title: Evaluating a Deterministic Validator Plus Single‑Iteration Repair Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (N=300 paired intent→configuration tasks; preregistration id cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1, preregistration SHA-256 archived) to evaluate whether a minimal guarded pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) followed by a frozen deterministic configuration validator and at most one automated repair iteration—reduces first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation. Execution completed 600 episodes and used 301 model calls. Observed outcomes: baseline = 299/300 valid (99.667%); guarded = 300/300 valid (100.0%); paired counts n11=299, n10=1, n01=0, n00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; absolute paired difference = 0.0033333; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). The single permitted automated repair corrected the sole invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]). The preregistered planning assumption used for power calculations (planned baseline pass rate = 0.40) was contradicted by the observed near‑ceiling baseline, removing statistical headroom for the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. We report preregistered design choices, compact execution accounting, confirmatory statistics, a post‑hoc inferential sensitivity bound tied to the archived contingency counts, and artifact‑grounded recommendations for future NetOps confirmatory evaluations. All run artifacts and analysis outputs are archived in the execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement.

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent into device configuration with generative models could materially speed NetOps workflows; however, incorrect or misordered device commands may produce outages or safety violations. Recent literature therefore recommends coupling probabilistic generators (LLMs) with deterministic verifiers or simulators (generate→verify→repair) as an operational floor‑safety pattern. Despite demonstrations and architectural proposals, there is limited preregistered paired evidence measuring how a narrow guarded pipeline affects first‑pass misconfiguration rates under controlled sampling semantics. We implement a narrowly scoped confirmatory study that evaluates: given a single LLM candidate per task, does a frozen deterministic validator plus at most one automated repair iteration reduce first‑pass misconfiguration relative to plain single‑shot generation? Our contributions are (1) a preregistered paired experiment with deterministic seeds and archival of all model outputs and validator/repair traces, (2) confirmatory statistics computed from archived artifacts, (3) a concise post‑hoc sensitivity quantification linked to the observed contingency counts, and (4) artifact‑grounded recommendations for planning future NetOps confirmatory experiments.
sections.related_work: Empirical and systems papers show LLMs can synthesize configuration templates or translate intent into device commands in controlled settings, while also documenting systematic failure modes—hallucination, misordering, and overconfidence—that threaten operational safety [10.1002/nem.2313]. Work on verifier‑assisted pipelines, retrieval‑assisted grounding, and bounded repair loops has reduced factual errors in adjacent domains (medical QA, code repair), motivating similar guarded architectures for NetOps [10.36227/techrxiv.176784505.56675782/v1, 10.2139/ssrn.6608518]. Classic network verification techniques (header‑space and specification‑based checking) provide algorithmic foundations for deterministic validators capable of static reachability and policy checks [10.1145/3098822.3098834]. Surveys and architectural proposals emphasize auditability and governance but note that production‑scale evidence for autonomous configuration execution without strong human oversight remains weak [10.36227/techrxiv.177004277.71795055/v1]. Our experiment occupies the intersection of these strands by providing a preregistered paired measurement of a minimal generate→validate→repair pipeline using a deterministic validator.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and hypotheses: We preregistered the study as cand-2026-001-A-prereg-v1 prior to observing outcomes. Confirmatory hypotheses were: H1 — the guarded pipeline reduces first‑pass misconfiguration rate by ≥50% (relative) versus single‑shot generation; H2 — one or fewer automated repair iterations recover ≥75% of initially invalid configurations. The preregistration explicitly used a numeric planning assumption baseline pass rate = 0.40 for power calculations; that literal value was used to motivate the N selection and the ≥50% relative reduction target. Design and sampling semantics: We used a paired within‑task design with a fixed deterministic seed list of 300 tasks. For each seed the same sampled LLM candidate was reused in both arms (shared_initial_candidate semantics): baseline (single‑shot generation) and guarded (the identical candidate validated and—if invalid—subjected to up to one automated repair attempt). The shared‑candidate semantics were preregistered to isolate the validator/repair intervention’s effect on a single generated plan; this design choice increases within‑pair correlation and reduces the number of informative discordant pairs available to McNemar inference relative to independent draws. Execution contract and limits: The declared model was gpt-5-mini and the frozen deterministic validator/repair adapter used the implementation identified in the run as deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. Missingness and retry policy: one retry was permitted per the preregistration; per the registered missingness plan the primary analysis treated only pairs with both calls failed as missing ('complete_pair_primary'). Scoring: The deterministic validator performs rule/dependency checks and canonicalizes outputs to normalized ASTs; a response is scored as a success only when the validator confirms all required command sequences and dependency constraints. Primary estimand and analysis: The primary estimand was paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistered primary test was the exact McNemar two‑sided test (α=0.05). We additionally preregistered estimation of the absolute risk difference with a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; bootstrap seed = 1729) and planned conditional analyses for repair success with exact binomial intervals.
sections.results: Execution accounting and archival: The run completed the preregistered episodes (planned = 600, completed = 600) and analyzed 300 complete pairs. The execution used 301 model calls (shared initial generation = 300, repair stage invocations = 1) and recorded zero provider/infrastructure failures per the preregistered retry policy. All normalized responses, validator decisions, and repair traces were archived in the execution manifest and analysis artifact bundle referenced in the Disclosure Statement and were the direct data source for the counts below. Primary outcome counts (artifact-derived): Baseline_success_count = 299/300 (99.667%); Guarded_success_count = 300/300 (100.0%). Paired contingency counts (guarded vs baseline): n11 = 299 (both success), n10 = 1 (guarded success, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (guarded fail, baseline success), n00 = 0 (both fail). Confirmatory inference (preregistered): Exact McNemar two‑sided test on these counts yields p = 1.00. Observed absolute paired difference (guarded minus baseline) = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033333. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.01] (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729). Repair outcomes (H2): the single allowed automated repair invocation corrected the single invalid baseline output (repair success 1/1); Clopper–Pearson 95% CI for 1/1 = [0.025, 1.0], reflecting wide uncertainty from a single observed repair case. Post‑hoc sensitivity bound (artifact‑grounded): the observed discordant total n10 + n01 = 1 imposes a hard upper bound on resolvable absolute paired difference equal to 1/300 ≈ 0.00333 under the run's sampling semantics with shared candidates. Consequently, the preregistered target effect corresponding to a ≥50% relative reduction (planned using baseline pass rate = 0.40 → planned absolute improvement ≈ 0.30) is incompatible with the observed contingency counts: detecting that preregistered effect would have required roughly 90 net discordant pairs in favor of guarded outputs. Diagnostic artifacts and verification: per‑task validator traces archived for each episode include normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, and repair_applied flags; the single corrected baseline case shows the validator flagging violations on the shared candidate and the repair adapter producing a post‑repair normalized configuration that satisfied all required constraints. All analysis artifacts supporting these statements are enumerated in the execution manifest cited in the Disclosure Statement.
sections.discussion: Interpretation and practical implications: The guarded pipeline corrected the only invalid baseline output in this run, showing that a frozen deterministic validator plus a bounded automated repair iteration can remediate validator‑detected violations in at least some cases. However, the run does not provide confirmatory evidence supporting the preregistered large relative effect (≥50%) because the observed baseline pass rate (299/300) contradicted the planning assumption (baseline = 0.40) and left effectively no statistical headroom. Design lessons for future confirmatory NetOps experiments: (1) calibrate task difficulty to achieve a targeted initial‑failure prevalence or targeted discordant‑pair count consistent with the planned effect size—the traditional sample‑size rationale should explicitly account for expected discordant counts under pairing semantics; (2) preregister pairing semantics and repair budgets and incorporate their impact on expected discordant pairs into power calculations (shared candidate reduces informative discordances; independent draws increase discordant potential); (3) when operational claims require runtime guarantees, integrate emulation or simulation that exercises packet‑level or control‑plane consequences rather than relying solely on static validators; (4) treat repair effectiveness as a conditional estimand (conditional on initial failure) and power the study for sufficient failure counts to estimate that quantity precisely. Threats to validity: Internal validity is affected by the preregistered shared_initial_candidate choice, which increases within‑pair correlation and reduces discordant information for McNemar tests. Construct validity is limited because the deterministic validator performs static canonical checks rather than live execution; runtime effects (e.g., transient traffic disruption) were not measured. External validity is limited by the synthetic task bank, vendor‑template scope, single model (gpt-5-mini), and single validator implementation. Conclusion validity is constrained by the small number of informative discordant pairs (one), producing wide uncertainty for conditional repair effectiveness and preventing confirmation of the preregistered large effect. Operational recommendation summary: for claims about large reductions in misconfiguration rates, researchers should (a) design task banks or adversarial perturbations to yield sufficient initial failures, (b) make pairing semantics and repair budgets explicit in preregistration, and (c) where deployment claims are important, include emulation that measures runtime semantic consequences.
sections.conclusion: We ran a preregistered paired experiment (N=300 pairs) assessing a minimal guarded pipeline (single‑shot gpt-5-mini candidate + frozen deterministic validator + ≤1 automated repair). Baseline single‑shot generation yielded 299/300 valid outputs; the guarded pipeline yielded 300/300 valid outputs; the single automated repair corrected the only observed baseline failure. However, because the observed baseline rate contradicted the preregistered planning assumption (baseline = 0.40), the study lacked the discordant‑pair evidence required to confirm the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction target. The run demonstrates precise artifacted execution and archival of model responses, validator traces, and repair traces, and it suggests concrete preregistration and task‑bank calibration practices required for future confirmatory NetOps evaluations that aim to resolve operationally large effect sizes.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and constrained vendor‑template scope limit external validity to broad production environments.
Single LLM (gpt-5-mini) and a single validator implementation restrict generality across model families and validator designs.

The preregistered power plan assumed a baseline pass rate = 0.40; the observed baseline (299/300) contradicted that assumption and removed statistical headroom to detect the preregistered ≥50% relative reduction.
Sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) reused the same initial candidate across paired arms, increasing within‑pair correlation and reducing discordant pairs available to McNemar inference.

Validation used deterministic configuration/constraint checks rather than full dynamic emulation of runtime semantic effects; actual runtime consequences of configurations were not executed and remain unmeasured.

H2 repair‑success evidence is based on a single initially invalid case (1/1 → 100%), yielding a wide Clopper–Pearson 95% CI = [0.025, 1.0]; larger counts of initial failures are required to estimate repair effectiveness precisely.
